utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC

utterances.speaker: MS. FAVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Natacha Faveau-Ivanovic for General Miletic, together with my assistant Nikolic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic and Natalie Wagner for Milan Gvero.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Your Honour: Peter Haynes, Djordje Sarapa, and Francesco Rindi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you Mr. Haynes, and good morning to you and your team. So let me start off with the left over from yesterday's sitting. Towards the end of the sitting, Mr. Krgovic, for Accused Gvero, raised what we considered to be an important matter related to the timing of the filing of exhibits or documents that are meant or intended to be used at cross-examination -- during cross-examination. We had left it at that yesterday, expecting the Prosecution to ponder about it and come back this morning with some kind of response. Do you take a position on that, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm sorry to say I didn't fully understand the argument yesterday, and I -- if you could restate the issue, I'm sure I can provide a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Would you like to do that yourself, Mr. Krgovic, or shall I do it for you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, given the fact that we have been using e-court, the documents that have been used in cross-examination would be submitted to the Prosecutor in hard copy once the witness took his solemn declaration and started to be examined. Since we have now been using this new system, the Defence team for General Gvero suggests that the same thing should be done for e-court, meaning at the moment when the witness starts testifying on direct, that these documents should be released on e-court and delivered to the Prosecution in that form, once the witness takes his solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. -- so much, Mr. Krgovic. Mr. McCloskey, what I suggest is the following: What was suggested or was -- what is at the back of -- in the background of Mr. Krgovic's submission is a decision handed down by Trial Chamber III in the Milutinovic trial on the 16th of August, which regulates this matter. It regulates it in a way which, in the mind of Mr. Krgovic, is commendable. So what we are suggesting is that you have a look at this decision - I can make it available and then you can let me have it back - and then after the first break please come back with some kind of response. Our position so far is that we think that the decision in Milutinovic is commendable, too. So I suggest that you have a look at it. Usher, please. And then later on in the day you can come back to deal with it. The other thing I wanted to mention is that my understanding is that when you finish with your opening statement, it will be then Mr. Ostojic, for Accused Beara, who will go first. And he will then be followed, as agreed, by Mr. Bourgon or Madam Nikolic, and the statement by Mr. Gvero will come at a later stage, when the opening statements are concluded. All right. Thank you. You have as much time as you need, and of course the time limit that will be allowed for the Defence will be regulated accordingly in the same manner. Yes, Mr. McCloskey, unless there are other preliminary issues that you would like to address. I see none. Yes, Mr. McCloskey. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We left off yesterday going over some of the key documents for General Miletic. I will continue. I would like to take you first to a -- what's referred to as a 13 July Main Staff VRS army report to the president of the Republika Srpska. Now, Ms. Stewart will put that up on the stand and blow it up a bit so we can especially see the heading at the top so that you can see what that is. This is what is fundamental to -- again, to the brigades, the corps, and the Main Staff. It was required for each of these units to send reports to their superior command, and this is a little different since this is the Main Staff sending their report to the office of the Presidency, to Radovan Karadzic. We have a large collection of these particular Main Staff reports and we -- for the year of 1995, and they -- many of them, in fact most of them for that year, are under the name of General Miletic, or Colonel Miletic, standing in for the Chief of Staff. There are some that Milovanovic himself writes, but for our period of time we mostly see General Miletic sending these important reports to the president. Now, these reports are the goings-on in all the different corps on a daily basis, and clearly it would take quite a bit of staff work for this to be assembled and sent on to the corps, so we are not suggesting that General Miletic would have written every word of this himself, though as a good general and a good staff officer he should be aware of the high points and would be aware of the high points. This is crucial information for the president to have, and I'll show you some of the information. Going directly to the 13th, if we could now go to page 3, paragraph 6(a). If we could blow up paragraph 6(a) so we can get a good read of it. This is, again, the Drina Corps section, and it's a report on what's going on in the Srebrenica area. And it says: "The enemy from the former enclave of Srebrenica is in a state of total disarray and troops are surrendering in large numbers to the VRS. A 200 to 300-strong group of soldiers managed to break through to the general sector of Mount Udrc, from where they are trying to break through to the territory under Muslim control." This is the kind of critical information that this general would and should be aware of. And you can see how important this information is. This is bad information. Two to three hundred. It was much more like to 5 to 6.000, and this was the first bit of bad intelligence that was getting up to the president's office that caused a lot of the distress later on. But this shows that General Miletic is aware of the situation, he's monitoring the situation, he's reporting the situation. These are all key elements in getting the job done, which, as you know, includes moving out the population. In fact, if we go down to paragraph 2, situation in the territory, if we blow that up: "There is an organised and planned transfer of the population from Srebrenica to the territory under Muslim control." He uses just about every word except "forcible" in there. Again, this shows -- this is important information, he is reporting basically what is the commission of a crime to the president. He is a key link in the information chain. It's not -- command bunkers are targeted for a good reason; to stop this kind of vital information so decisions don't get made with proper information and armies collapse. General Miletic is a key member of that staff, passing on key information to the Presidency. He would have, of course, been an excellent target, a military target, for any of the Muslim army. The next document I'd like to go to is a report dated 14 July from General Tolimir, and he's sending it from the command of the 1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade, sometimes better known as the Rogatica Brigade, whereas you recall from yesterday he had been sent by Mladic to look after the Zepa operation. And we note from that document -- if we could blow it up a bit. Maybe if you're sitting closer to it you can read it, but I can tell we're going to need to make that bigger. I know it's -- looking at the ELMO fondly, but I'll try to avoid it. This is to the Main Staff of the Republika Srpska personally to General Miletic. Now, this is something you will see not infrequently. When a general or an officer wants to make darn sure someone gets something, they say, "Personally to," because they know it's going to a staff, and in order to get that vital communication communicated, they will write "Personally to," and they do it obviously for a reason. And this one from Tolimir is obviously personally to General Miletic, so we know General Miletic is at the Main Staff, doing his job that day. And it is related to the protection of TVP, which is military information. And I won't read this to you, but you can tell that it has to do with connecting the Drina Corps communications network to the Main Staff so that everyone can be fully informed with the radio traffic. And this is General Tolimir providing key information to General Miletic, which is key information for the operation and shows how important both of them are. Neither of them are mere paper shufflers, technical people that aren't involved. The next document I would go to is a document that comes out of the Main Staff - again, if we could blow that up - on 15 July to the 1st Krajina Corps from General Miletic. And it says, "Chief of Staff's representative" down there. I believe that's just a mistranslation of "standing in for the Chief of Staff." Translation, as you know, can interpret things differently, but we will get this corrected before it becomes an exhibit. In any event -- and I won't spend the time to read this, but what this is is General Miletic notifying the Krajina Corps that they will send a unit to assist Zvornik. Now, this is the -- to assist in the combat operations. And unless we see evidence that it is involved in the murder operation or the forcible transfer operation, we give the reasonable doubt to the Defence. This appears to be in support of the combat operation. But it shows General Miletic sending troops and -- and it's in a firm command-like way. If you read this -- the language, the command shall do this, they shall do that, this is the kind of orders and directives that is normal for someone in this position, standing in for the Chief of Staff, to issue. These are orders, though, as we've said, technically the Chief of Staff cannot issue or originate orders. He would be doing this under his mantle that he has been authorised to do from his commander. All right. Now, this is an intercept dated 17 July, and it's -- involves Krstic and the commander. And the commander refers to Krstic as Krle. You will see on a video General Mladic referring to Krstic as Krle. This is his nickname that a few chosen people used, General Mladic one of them. Colonel Beara used it as well, as you'll see in another intercept. What we can see from this, if we can blow it up again so we can maybe read it a bit better: "Krstic: The commander ... "Hello. "Yes? "Krle, can you hear me?" Krstic: "I can hear you. "Full steam ahead." Krstic: "Understood." Commander: "Get in touch with Miletic on a secure line. Full steam ahead. I didn't accept the Turks' conditions." Krstic: "Understood. "Bye." Now, this has to do with Zepa. On the 17th of July there are negotiations, if you can call them that, they are not really negotiations, but they are between Mladic and the BiH officials, and they go on for a few days before this is finally resolved in a certain way on the 27th. And what Mladic is doing is he's calling Krstic, the man who's in charge of the attack on Zepa, to let him know first and foremost he did not accept the conditions - you'll see that there are various agreements that are discussed during the Zepa case - and that the first thing he wants Krstic to do is get in touch with Miletic and tell him that. Miletic is at the command post likely. He is the man at home that needs to know what's going on. Krstic is the command of the operation, is the first man that needs to know. Miletic is the coordinator, as the chief of operations and standing in for the Chief of Staff, is the next man that needs to know. And that shows the important role that each of these individuals is playing. All right. Lastly, I have another document from Tolimir, this one dated 21 July, and this also having to do with Zepa. Tolimir is writing from the Podrinje Brigade. And again, it's to General Miletic. Can you blow that up chunk by chunk so they can see it. It's to General Miletic personally, and it's the situation on Zepa. And I won't go through all of this, but it basically talks about the Muslims organising the defence in certain areas and that they have -- using the UNPROFOR flak jackets and combat equipment and are targeting UNPROFOR to try to provoke NATO's reaction and up to antics to confuse the Serb enemy. Then he says: "I propose to ban the arrival of representatives of UNPROFOR and international organisations in the zone of combat operations for mediation in negotiations." That's number 3. This is important so they can control the situation. And then number 4: "We believe that it is more profitable to hold direct negotiations after inflicting losses on the enemy's manpower. We ask you to provide" a means to do this, basically. Then the second paragraph says: "It would be most profitable to destroy them by using chemical means, or aerosol mines and bombs. By using these means, we would cause the fall of Zepa and surrender of the Moslems. We will continue combat operations with direct attack weapons to break through in the mentioned directions." This is an assistant commander making a proposal to use chemical weapons. Now, there's a lot about chemical weapons in the news, but there are different kinds of chemical weapons. The JNA and the VRS had some pretty ugly stuff; however, they also had material that was called -- I believe it's called CS, and it's fundamentally tear gas. And while the investigation has not borne out the exact kind of chemical weapons suggested here, I -- it appears more likely that they're talking about tear gas as opposed to some of the more psychotropic drugs that are much more dangerous, but the investigation is still working on that. But at this point, again, I would look at this more as tear gas than I would as anything more extreme. However, the next paragraph - and if we could blow this one up - this is a different story. "We believe that by destroying the refugee columns of Muslim population from directions of Stublici, Radave, and Brloske Planine, we would force the Muslims to surrender quickly." Now, this is General Tolimir. He wants to bomb the Muslim civilian refugee columns to force them to surrender, and he's telling this to his colleague General Miletic. Now, you don't talk this kind of criminal trash to someone that is not part of your organisation and part of your mind-set. This kind of horrendous criminal proposal goes to General Miletic for a purpose. He's the man that will deal with it. And we know from the facts of Zepa that certainly the civilian population was targeted. Let me go on to General Gvero. Now, as the assistant commander for legal, religious, and moral affairs, it's a difficult position to define, even for the VRS officers I've asked. At the brigade level, most of the assistant commanders are dealing with the funerals and the arrangements with the families of lost soldiers, and with issues, of course, related to law and religion. At the level of the Main Staff, General Gvero deals with similar issues sometimes, but it appears he's mainly dealing with media issues, propaganda issues, dealing with the international forces, and he seems to be a jack-of-all-trades for General Mladic, and we'll point to certain individual documents that show that and you'll hear more about this from the evidence. So the first document I'd like to go to is another document from Tolimir. And this is a document I made reference to. It's an important historical document, because as it's dated July 9th, it appears to go out, if you look at the date stamp, very late; 2350 hours. And it is -- it says: "Very urgent to the President of Republika Srpska for information and the Drina Corps IKM." That means forward command post. You'll be hearing "IKM" over and over again; that means forward command post. And again we see this Generals Gvero and Krstic personally. Now, we know that, and you'll see other evidence, that Generals Krstic and Gvero are at the Pribicevac forward command post of the Srebrenica operation, and that's why this is being sent to them. And this is basically, as I said before, an indication that the president has now decided to take the enclave. And so that critical information is going to Gvero and Krstic personally. And you will note they are no longer concerned about the UN, they are no longer concerned about NATO -- I'm sure they're still very much concerned but not so much to hold them up. They now decide to go anyway. And interesting to look at the last two paragraphs are -- they want to ensure safety of the UNPROFOR members and the Muslim population, they want to guarantee the Geneva Conventions are in place, and this is -- and that is something that Tolimir is stressing. The same fellow that wants to bomb the refugees, and the same army that at the time that this is going on has -- is now holding Dutch hostages and has targeted the Srebrenica civilian population during their attack. And on the 11th, two days after this, they threaten to kill the Dutch hostages if NATO drops any more bombs. So I think you should take a good look at this document, but I think you will see it for what it really is. And -- but again, as it pertains to General Gvero, it shows how important he is. He is Mladic's man in Srebrenica. He is there so the key decisions can be made on whether to attack or whether or not to attack. Krstic, of course, is commanding the operation, but Gvero is Mladic's eyes and ears to the operation. Okay. The next document I'm going to is -- it's got a couple of dates on it; 10 July on the left side on the top, and 10 June on the right side. It's referring to the events of Srebrenica up till about 10 or 11 July, so it's clearly coming from that July time period. And it's -- comes from the information service of the Republika Srpska Main Staff. And as you can see, it is coming from Lieutenant-General Milan Gvero. I won't go over all of it today. The first page is a synopsis of Srebrenica and the examples of how the Muslims have been violating the truce and that the enclaves were never demilitarised and that they constantly attacked outside of the villages, outside the enclave, which is all true. As you read it, you'll see the tone of it is somewhat inflammatory. It's directed to vilify the Muslims and in an inflammatory propagandist tone, but fundamentally the information in it is true. And then we get to the second page and it goes on to the more recent events, many of which are also true, again the same tone. And then the last half of the page, where it begins: "They also killed a United Nations soldier ..." This is true, as you recall from yesterday. "UNPROFOR, although fully aware of the Muslim terrorists as well as the complete military actions, does not prevent them." Now he's going into what unfortunately become a similar refrain, referring to Muslims as terrorists. Now, there were some terrorists among the BiH army and they did some terrible things, but the tone of this is that Muslims and Islam amounts to terror and they are terrorists. Then he goes on to say: "Our combat activities at the moment are directed towards simply neutralising the Muslim terrorists and are in no way directed against civilians or members of UNPROFOR." This is flat out not true. They have directed their attack at the civilians and at UNPROFOR, driving UNPROFOR from their OPs and dropping shells around the UNPROFOR base, basically terrorising UNPROFOR as well as the civilian population. "Some UNPROFOR members, for their own safety, have crossed into our territory and are our guests now, well sheltered and safe." Well, they are at the Hotel Fontana, they are being looked after, they are being filmed, they are being used as propaganda pawns at this time, so he is right. The next day, when NATO drops bombs, they are told, "You keep doing that, NATO, and we are going to kill these men." This is used in combination, propaganda and strategy the next day. It's all part of the ongoing operation to get his public behind him and get the word out to the world in a false way to allow their job to be easier. Then he gets into his last paragraph and kind of an ugly talk about foreigners, media, and says: "In Srebrenica the main decisions are made by people of little strength and intelligence. Their advisers from an Islamic centre are just the same." Saying the enemy is stupid is designed to demean the enemy, designed to raise the furor of the public and the soldiers. This is the kind of thing that leads to war crimes. All right. Now I'd like to go to an intercept, and I believe it is dated the 11th of July, and it's between General Gvero and President Karadzic. And they can't hear Karadzic, so all these words are Gvero. Gvero says: "I just talked to Nicolai." Now, Nicolai is the UNPROFOR Dutch general who was in charge at the time. "I just talked to that General Nicolai. "We asked for ... He wants to - he says, stop attacking the UN. I told him that his information is probably from Muslims and that we haven't attacked the UN. I'm asking him to stop the operation immediately and get those planes out of our sky, and as far as the UN, if they were fired on at all, then they were fired on by those who they are protecting: the Muslims. And if they are under threat, they should cross over to us and they'll be safe. "That's right, I told him, Mr. President. "Everything is going according to plan, don't worry." General Gvero is fully engaged in the plan, he's speaking directly to the president of the Republika Srpska, he's passing on his propaganda lies that he's telling to UNPROFOR. This is at a time when they have threatened or are about to threaten the death of UN soldiers. This shows General Gvero fully connected to the command structure and fully involved in the operation that will lead to the take-down of the enclave and the eventual movement out of the Muslim population. All right. Another intercept between Gvero and Karadzic. Same thing; all you get is Gvero. "President, Serbian silver, the Serbian church, the Serbian flag." Srebrenica is famous for silver mines. So he is again still in touch with President Karadzic, telling him the Serbian flag is flying at the Serbian church, and that's Srebrenica. Now, another report from 11 July, and this is to the Drina Corps headquarters and the Drina Corps forward command post from General Gvero, from the Main Staff. And it's a very -- and it's entitled: "Warning on the treatment of UNPROFOR and personnel in the enclave of Srebrenica." I won't read it all, but it's a very strict and tough direction to not be rude or do anything bad against the UNPROFOR. And in the end, it says why: "Such attitude towards UNPROFOR units are at this moment of multifarious importance for the realisation of the assignment at hand and of our set objectives." It's not because it's humanitarian, it's because it meets our objectives. Multifarious. I'd love to hear the Bosnian word for that. But that's classic Gvero thinking. It shows the power he has. He's the man at the command post. Mladic is walking through Srebrenica. Tolimir is at Zepa. Milovanovic is at the Krajina. Miletic is also at the command post, but probably doing more work. All right. Let's go now to a 13 July order, again from the Main Staff, under the hand of Milan Gvero. This is actually entitled: "Order." As an assistant commander he is not empowered to make orders, but as a top Main Staff general, Mladic may authorise him to make such orders, and he obviously felt comfortable, either with Mladic's direct authority or authority on his own, to send out this order regarding the capture of the people in the column. And I -- again, I won't go through it all, but I want to point out the first big paragraph. And it says: "Based on the instructions received and following the defeat in the Srebrenica enclave, the men from the enclave fit for military service were tasked with crossing over to Tuzla and Kladanj in groups and carrying weapons. Among them are inveterate criminals and villains who will stop at nothing just to avoid being captured and reach Muslim-controlled territory." Now, remember when I said you lead by example. This group has got women in it, it's got a few kids, two-thirds of it is not armed. You'll see a picture of this rag-tag group. The first quarter or third of it is armed and is tough and has killed some Serbs, so no problem there. But when you describe a group to your soldiers as inveterate criminals and villains, "among them are inveterate criminals and villains," you're asking them, you're giving them the green light to commit crimes. This is not the way he was trained. None of these men were trained to write this kind of thing; it's what occurred after this war started and it's what led to these crimes. All right. Another --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I'm not sure whether this is an appropriate time, but if I can ask this: How do you suggest we would follow your opening statement if we are to read it later on? You haven't published these documents. You haven't given the reference number. Any idea?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would be privileged for you to read my opening statement. I don't think you have to. I think the evidence will speak for it. We will provide you with all of these documents in the order that they are spoken of, and the date -- the date and nature of my first description of them is actually pretty good because the -- and especially if you have them in a packet. I can give that packet to the Defence and to the Judges without any problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So I would appreciate if you could give it -- try to produce at least a list of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. I think that's a good point. Mr. Bourgon made a similar point this morning and we were looking at 65 ter numbers, but it seemed a little rough so I decided not to do that. But I take your point, but we will provide you with that -- with that list and the documents themselves, if that's preferable. Also, as I mentioned prior to trial, it's our intention to provide the Court and the Defence, as soon as we can finish it, binders on the key documents, the key intercepts, and a short synopsis of the key evidence of -- for each accused and provide that to the binders [sic]. And this is what this case will be all about. I think that will be very valuable. We have not finished with it. I hope to finish with it soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And please interrupt me at any time and ask questions. This, of course, may be -- well, you can always ask, as you know, questions any time, but given that many of these issues we won't get to for several months and that these are the issues that this case will be tried upon, I certainly appreciate any questions. I may not have the answer but I can try to direct you to the future evidence. As you know, nothing I say now is evidence. All right. Now I'm going to a document dated 17 July, 1995. It's to the Main Staff of the VRS, to General Milan Gvero, assistant commander for morale, religious, and legal affairs, and it's from the president, Radovan Karadzic. And he's basically chewing out Gvero. And this is what he said, and I won't read all the dates and orders that he says Gvero has violated, but I hope you'll get the gist of this. "Despite my order reference number -" and then lots of dates - "referring to the prevention of the drain of secret information, my directive ... dated December 5 regarding contacts with international organisations ... April 3rd about making contacts with foreigners ..." Another order of May 31 and January, 1995, "regarding the means of information," then "regarding the work of the State Committee for Cooperation with the UN and International Humanitarian Organisations. "You are acting contrary to all these mandatory documents. "You have sabotaged the order pertaining to the Information Ministry's exclusive task of information, which inflicted serious propaganda-related damage, both domestically and abroad. You supplied information outside the assigned channels. You made unauthorised contact with international organisations without the presence and permission of authorised state organs and made decisions about the evacuation of the sick and injured, for which the State Committee for Cooperation with the UN and International Humanitarian Organisations is in charge. "Considering everything mentioned herein, and pursuant to Article 80 of the constitution of Republika Srpska and amendment 40 to the constitution, I hereby order: "1. Immediately send a written statement about this non-compliance with an order and exceeding authority, following which you will be called for an interview to give a personal explanation." Now, the first part of this was mostly stuff we've been hearing about, his contact with international organisations, his dealing with propaganda issues, seriously affected Karadzic. So these were not just silly little press releases and other things. But we also see that, according to Karadzic, he made decisions about the evacuation of the sick and injured. And we see some evidence that he's involved in a meeting with organisations about that. So he's clearly involved in that as well. Amazingly enough, we have a copy of General Gvero's response. It's short and to the point. And it's also dated 17 July from the Main Staff -- excuse me, it's dated 18th July from the Main Staff regarding the subject of the 17 July document from Karadzic. And it says, if we could blow up that part: "I have carried out all the activities mentioned in your document as ordered by my immediate superior - the commander of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. "All the ... were carried out and motivated by the need for the fight of the Serbian people and the army to be successful, as can be seen from the success of the VRS in Srebrenica, Zepa, and on other fronts." This is the theme of the Prosecution's case. Gvero is following the orders of Mladic and ordered to be successful in Srebrenica and Zepa. He's playing a substantial role, a key role, and that role is not just to take them down militarily but to move out the population, knowing that people would be killed, people would die. There were foreseeable consequences of that. He says it for us; unbelievable. Last document for General Gvero. This is another one of these reports from General Tolimir from the Rogatica Brigade area about Zepa. And it's dated 25 July. This is a few days before Zepa was semi-resolved. And it's to the Main Staff of the army, personally to General Gvero or General Miletic. Very interesting that Tolimir is looking at these guys as semi-interchangeable. Miletic is the Chief of Staff, standing in for the Chief of Staff, doing all that work; Gvero is helping out and doing the work that you've seen him do. They both have similar hats for Mladic, and they're the key guys to talk to. Milovanovic, again, is in the Krajina, the corps commanders are at their fronts. So that's important to see how key these guys are. Now, this is talking about the Muslims and accepting an agreement, though I don't think the agreement has finally been hashed out yet. Various discussions about the state commission on war prisoners. During this time the Muslims are very much concerned that if they turn themselves in, they are also with the ICRC getting registered, and the Serbs are fighting it. But number 2 is the interesting part, paragraph 2, if we could blow that up. "The Muslims demand that General Gobillar --" Now, General Gobillar is a French general high up in the command of UNPROFOR at that time. "The Muslims demand that General Gobillar comes to Zepa as UNPROFOR representative and representatives of ICRC. "Pass on to UNPROFOR a request to send an officer of a colonel rank from Sarajevo Sector to UNPROFOR check-point 2 -" that's at Zepa, by the way - "at Boksanica to monitor the execution of the agreement." So he doesn't want a colonel -- or he doesn't want a general, he wants a colonel. And then the next paragraph: "Make a note to them that we don't want them to send a general considering that we have information that they want to take advantage of his presence according the similar scenario when they took advantage of the presence of General Morillon in Srebrenica in 1993." Tolimir is sending this to Gvero and Miletic. They all very clearly remember General Morillon stepping in and saving the Muslim population from the Serb army and the onslaught, and they don't want the same thing happening in Zepa. Keep the French generals out of here; we'll take a colonel. And sending that on to these guys. They think historically; they are remembering the past. And this shows Gvero, Miletic, Tolimir, all of them acting in their positions, as they should, getting the job done, taking down -- disabling the UNPROFOR forces so that they can control the situation. Now, in Zepa the men never reached an agreement because the VRS was never able to satisfy them that they wouldn't be harmed, and so they ended up some 500-plus, thousand swimming across the Drina River or taking rafts or boats or wheelbarrows on logs and getting to Serbia around the latter part of July and August, whereupon the Red Cross showed up and started registering them. And so if you made it to Serbia in early August, you survived. Some 500 to a thousand men survived because they got to Serbia and the Red Cross got involved. Now, whether the Red Cross was there and was able to get involved before Milosevic and his forces could do anything about it, or whether Milosevic sent them and took advantage as a propaganda ploy is the subject of another trial at another time, which, as we all know, did not finish. You'll see intercepts directly related to the events going across to Serbia. It's been about an hour, and that was my last item for General Gvero, so I think it's a good time to stop, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I thank you, Mr. McCloskey. We'll have a break of 20 minutes, starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey, you may proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay. Now we're on to General Pandurevic, at the time a Colonel Pandurevic, the commander of the Zvornik Brigade. As I've briefly alluded, he was leading a task force of the top Zvornik Brigade units and was one of the key assaulting units. And I want to show you just a still from a photograph -- still from a video that you'll see with Mr. Ruez's testimony. And this is a still from the approach from the south, from Zeleni Jadar, down -- getting close to Srebrenica. And you'll see that we have General Mladic in the forefront. To his left is General Krstic, body-guard next to General Krstic, and to Mladic's right is Vinko Pandurevic. You'll see the video clip with General Mladic together with General Krstic and Pandurevic as they make a triumphant walk through Srebrenica. And at one point Mladic, who knows the camera is in front of him, is saying: "On to Potocari, on to Bratunac." And you'll see Colonel Pandurevic lean over to him and says something to the effect that, General, the Muslims are -- we have to get the Browning up on the hills, the Browning meaning the Browning machine-gun, in order to help secure the area, that we shouldn't just walk down this valley until it's secured. So Colonel Pandurevic is thinking like the general that he is. Krstic is standing back quiet, not saying anything, and Pandurevic is the one that has the courage to look at Mladic and tell him that, you know, there's more that needs to be done, and Mladic basically says: Do what you need to do. I mention that because clearly there is a character and courage there. And I would say that General Pandurevic would be a general you would want to defend your village in other times, but not in this war. He had the courage to be a part general and didn't lack the courage to be a real general, and you'll see that throughout. Now, I want to go to the one document for General Pandurevic, it's the most important document in the case against Pandurevic; it is the veritable smoking-gun document. It shows him in charge, with knowledge of the prisoners in his zone, and knowing what's going on with them. Now, I'll go over this document because, like all documents, it takes some interpretation. It is what's called an interim combat report. Now, the way the system worked was they had regular combat reports that were due in the afternoon, I believe, early evening; and then when something special came up, they wrote what is called or what we translate as interim combat reports for special, urgent situations. We don't have all the interim combat reports to the Presidency, we have all the regular ones. But we have, we believe, all the interim combat reports from the Zvornik Brigade. We searched the Zvornik Brigade in 1998. It was one of the searches of any army ever. It was actually the second search. The first search was from the Krajina Corps in Banja Luka. A few weeks later we searched the Zvornik Brigade and got copies of many of these critical documents that had not been destroyed. And this document, we know from previous testimony from a Zvornik officer, was a document that was dictated to this officer by Pandurevic himself personally. So there's no question about this document, there's no question it came from Colonel Pandurevic. And taking you back to the -- this is the evening hours of 15 July. We look at a -- there's a stamp on it, if you want to look at the original, a sent stamp, that says it was sent at 1925 hours, so it would have been dictated sometime shortly before that, likely. And as you recall, at this time Pandurevic has been back in his brigade for several hours. He came back at about noon. He of course took a detailed report from Obrenovic, as detailed as it could be in this kind of combat situation and a situation where they had some 6.000 Muslim men that they had to kill. But he received that report, as I told you, regarding the -- both the combat events as well as the thousand prisoners in the school and the problems they would have guarding them and burying them. Sorry, a fly seems to have made its way into the courtroom. So after receiving Obrenovic's report about the thousands of Muslim men in the schools and the problems with guarding them and burying them and receiving the military situation, he is in -- he is in very dire straits. As I explained, the 2nd Corps is on his front, the 28th Division is at his rear. He has some 5 or 6.000 Muslim prisoners located in the schools in his area, guarded by his troops and being buried by his engineering units, the bulldozers, the men, the materials. I could go on and on and on about how much this takes of the Zvornik Brigade, and you'll see the logs and the references to all this material, but he knows all this. And he can tell the Muslims are gearing up for a final push towards Nezuk and towards them. And so that's the context by which he is writing this. And I'll go over it slowly with you because, as I say, it's the key document. It is to the -- his commander, which is of course normal, the Drina Corps command. "Since the fall of Srebrenica, in the territory of the 1st Zvornik Infantry Brigade area of responsibility, in the wider area of Pandurice, Planica, Crni Vrh, Kamenica, and Glodansko Brdo, there are about 3.000 armed and unarmed enemy soldiers." Recognises that this column has got some people who are armed and some who are not armed. 3.000 is probably an underestimate. It's probably more like 4.000, 5.000, 6.000. These numbers are impossible to get exactly, but within a reasonable intelligence figure, though he may tell us it's not reasonable given that it was off. 3.000 anyway; a large force. "Brigade forces are sealing off and searching the aforementioned region. A few hundred enemy soldiers have so far been liquidated." Now, "liquidated" is an English term that implies murder. I don't think that is a fair translation always in the context of the reports that we see. We occasionally see reports where they're referring to liquidating the enemy in what could be combat. So, as is our general habit, if there are potentially two reasonable interpretations, we will give them the benefit of the doubt. We also see the term "liquidation" referred to to what it precisely means in English. For example, you'll see documents coming out of, I believe it's the Rogatica or Visegrad Brigade, saying: Today we liquidated ten Muslims, and from them we learned the following, and then a long list of information they learned from their interrogation. In that context, liquidation clearly means: Today we murdered Muslims, but before we murdered them, we got this information. So in this -- at this point, I do not -- we do not -- Mr. Butler does not view this as that we have murdered 300. Also, as you may recall, by the evening of 15 July, there are some 1.000 Muslim men from Orahovac that are murdered -- have been murdered and are being in the process of buried, and there are some 1.000 men from Petkovci that have been murdered and are in the process of being buried. And by the evening of 15th July, they're just finishing up or they're still murdering some 500 to 1.000 people from the Rocevic school at the Kozluk, on the banks of the Drina River. So if he was silly enough to give them the exact figures on the number that they murdered, it would be more in the area of 2.500 to 3.000. So this figure of a few hundred enemy have been liquidated is probably a reference to enemy killed during -- in the woods. Now, whether it was combat in the woods or murder in the woods is difficult to tell. There was certainly combat going on in the woods at this time, though you will see murders of people in the woods that were certainly not combat related. But 300, that's probably an overestimate at this point. There had not been a major engagement, they had not suffered major losses, but clearly the number of enemy had been killed in the woods at this time, and that's what that refers to as far as we can tell. Then: "Throughout 15 July 1995, BH army forces of the Tuzla 2nd Corps launched fierce attacks on the brigade defence area in order to link up with the forces which had been cut off. The attack on the defence area of the 4th, 6th, 7th Battalions along the Petkovci-Memici stretch was launched at 0430, with simultaneous actions by the besieged forces." This is true. There were not serious casualties during this action, though being on the receiving end of artillery is, I'm sure, an ominous experience, and this is what this paragraph is reflecting. "Enemy attacks were vigorously supported by all calibres of artillery and tanks. Attacks of varying intensity followed one another from the direction of Nezuk and Kalesija on Memici. The attack on Memici is still in progress. All targets deep inside the territory, and the suburbs and town of Zvornik have all been under artillery fire. All attacks have been repulsed successfully so far. So far, according to information received, we have four dead and a dozen or so wounded." Not significant -- well, four people are significant, but the real losses have yet to come for the Serbs. "With all available forces, we have sealed off the wider area of Crni Vrh and Planica and partially the area of Kamenica. "All brigade forces are fully engaged and we have no reserves." And here are the two paragraphs that will be paragraphs that you will study and review and compare to the evidence throughout this case: "An additional burden for us is the large number of prisoners distributed throughout the schools in the brigade area, as well as obligations of security and sanitary-technical measures in the field. "This command cannot take care of these problems any longer, as it has neither the material nor other resources. If no one takes on this responsibility, I will be forced to let them go." Okay. At this time there's nobody left alive in the Orahovac school, there's nobody left alive at the Petkovci school. There may be a few left alive at the Rocevic school, but not many. But in Pilica there's at least 500 at the cultural centre in downtown Pilica. There's probably at least a thousand to 1.500 people jammed into the Kula school in Pilica, and it's there that they're having problems guarding them and shooting them, and it's a mess, and that's what he's referring to. It's what the duty officer of that day, Jokic, told Obrenovic about; Obrenovic told his commander. His commander is now reporting it up the chain of command. Now, as it says: "The additional burden for us is the large number of prisoners distributed throughout the schools in the brigade area." That's clear what that means; there's no other reasonable interpretation: He knows the prisoners are there. "... as well as obligations of security and sanitary-technical measures in the field." Now, obligations of security. You've heard the security branch has been made responsible for murdering the prisoners. And in the Serbian language the term "security" is used in two different ways: The security branch is one term and the term security for guarding people is another term. The term that is used in this document is the term to guard people. So I don't want to suggest that he's saying we have the obligations of the security branch, though he knows of that obligation. What he's referring to in this document is his obligation to secure those prisoners. He goes on and says: "And the sanitary-technical measures in the field." Now, the way that the term that is used -- and I'll read it in English and give you the Bosnian term because it's a term you need to become and you will become familiar with. "Distributed throughout the schools in the brigade area as well as obligations of security," and "asanacija." Now, "asanacija" is a Serbian military term that you will find in the Serbian military dictionary, and it refers to the cleaning-up of the battle-field, and it can refer to cleaning up animal dead, destroyed vehicles, and human dead. We see it referred to in this case in documents repeatedly as cleaning up the human dead. In fact, it's referred to the burial of the human dead. And we see -- for example, we see it in the notebook of the Bratunac Brigade in October during the reburial operation, which I haven't really mentioned much of. But clearly in the notebook Momir Nikolic has written down at the command meeting that: "Today we are engaged in tasks given to us by the Main Staff of asanacija," and that's the time that they are reburying everyone. So that's how it is generally used and that's how we see it used. Now, in this situation we know that at the time he says "asanacija" his engineering unit, with the help of the civilian protection, are still in the process of burying some thousands of prisoners that were killed in Orahovac. The -- many of the bulldozer drivers have testified and talk about that. You'll see it in the records of the engineering unit, going to Orahovac on the 14th, on the 15th, on the 16th. So these units are engaged in burying people at Orahovac. They're also burying people at the dam. You'll see the engineering unit talking about an ULT-220 being sent to the dam. ULT is a huge loader that has the ability to dig holes. So they're burying people at Petkovci at this time. They haven't started burying people at Kozluk, but they soon will have and they'll have a huge job to bury people at Branjevo Farm. So when he says, "as well as obligations of security and asanacija," what he's referring to is burying the dead. So he knows there are thousands of people in his schools, it is a huge burden to guard them, and that is a huge burden to bury them. At the same time, he's getting hit from the rear and the front and Zvornik's in place. This is the reason why we see this: He is under tremendous stress. And he writes it down and says it like it is. He's not happy with the situation by the tone of this, but he knows the situation. He knows precisely what's going on. And he knows that if you're guarding prisoners and you're burying prisoners, you darn well know you're killing them. And he has taken responsibility for this, as he says. And he says: If I don't get help doing it, I'm going to let these guys go, which means he's going to let the rest of the guys in Branjevo go. And if he had called the ICRC, they had gone to Pilica, right across the river, then those people would have been alive today. 1.500 people. He could have stopped the executions at Kozluk, another 500 to a thousand people. He didn't. He stayed on. It happened on his watch, with his troops, with his knowledge. He's the commander, he knows it, he takes responsibility for it. Okay. Let's go on to Mr. Borovcanin. I mentioned earlier that when he was assigned from his position in Sarajevo, it was on the 10th of July, and there's a document that shows that. This document is not in dispute. Mr. Borovcanin acknowledged this document and that it's truthful, and I'll go over it a bit. But it is dated on the 10th of July and it's under the hand of -- or the name of Tomislav Kovac, but I believe someone who signed it is signing it for him. And this is an indication that pursuant to the order of the supreme commander, Karadzic, this order is issued. So, as I mentioned before, in order to put the MUP under the command of the army, you had to get the authority of the president, so this is clearly what this is about. And it basically says that he detaches himself from the Sarajevo front and he goes with the following units: The 2nd Special Police Detachment from Sekovici - that's one unit of the special police from the outfit that he's from; the 1st Company of the PJP unit of the Zvornik SJB - that's the civilian outfit I talked about. CJB, SJB are used pretty much interchangeably for the civilian police organisations. A mixed company of the joint Republika of Serbian Krajina - that's what RSK means - Serbian and RS MUP forces and a company from the training camp at Jahorina. Now, Mr. Borovcanin told us that the Serbian MUP did not come with him, and we -- the investigation has not been able to identify any members of the Serbian MUP in the Srebrenica location that -- of the Srebrenica and Bratunac area of the Zvornik municipality. You know from the indictment, and I -- there were murders in Trnovo of Srebrenica victims in later July by these events by a member of the Serbian MUP, and those were people that Mr. Borovcanin was working with in Sarajevo. But we have not been able to confirm whether or not they came with him to Srebrenica. They were clearly back -- they were clearly a unit of the Skorpion from the Serbian MUP in Bosnia, killing Srebrenica victims, but we do not associate that directly in any way with Mr. Borovcanin. This Trnovo event seemed to be one of practicality, where there were buses that had come from the Sarajevo area and Muslim men must have been -- and this is speculation, Muslim men must have been put in the buses that were going back to Sarajevo anyway, because we know for a fact that people from Potocari, from the woods, were murdered in the Trnovo area and buried. It's on video. It's not a video I intend to show you today; you'll see it at some point. But we don't associate that, to be clear, with Mr. Borovcanin. Then it basically says he is to report with his unit to Bratunac 11 July, 1200 hours, and he's obliged to contact General Krstic. He is now under the command of General Krstic. All right. Let's go to another -- another document, another -- just a photo. You'll see Mr. Borovcanin on the photo. He had a cameraman that -- a quasi-journalist who would -- who was designated to go with him from Belgrade, and he was with him, filming much of Mr. Borovcanin's contact. Whether he filmed this one or if this is Serb TV, I don't know, but this particular shot is of Borovcanin on the 12th of July in front of the Muslims that are gathered there. And he is doing a propaganda stunt, handing out chocolate to the children. You will hear testimony from Dutch soldiers that after the cameras were turned off some of the Serb soldiers came and took away the chocolate. But this is clearly a propaganda stunt, showing that he is part of the propaganda operation. And there in Potocari, where troops under his command are present and assisting in the separation of the women and children and present when the brutality of Potocari is occurring. Okay. The next photograph is a photograph of Mr. Borovcanin, and the man in the beret, the black man, is Major Kingori. He's a United Nations military observer from Kenya. And there -- this is on the 13th of July. This is shot by Mr. Petrovic, the journalist from Belgrade. And they are discussing various things and the organisation of what is going on. Mr. Borovcanin is active on the ground, in command on Potocari both days, 12th and 13th, in the middle of this horrendous crime scene of deportation and abuses of the public. You may recall seeing the shot and -- of the Muslim men standing on the balcony of the famous white house. Well, Mr. Borovcanin is standing in this photograph that -- that we're looking at, is standing in front of the white house, facing those men on the balcony. You'll see when it's panned that first they start with him there and then they pan to the white house, so he's looking right at the men that are jammed on that house. All right. Then Mr. Borovcanin later goes along, with his cameraman, along the Bratunac-Milici road, where the various crimes I have mentioned occurred, Kravica principally, and I did not mention the crimes of Nova Kasaba a little farther down the road, but they also occurred there, as described in the indictment. I didn't mention the crime in Sandici, that after Kravica in the evening, about 16 people were still at the meadow that didn't have transportation anywhere, and the Jahorina unit, called the deserter unit because they were made up of a bunch of men that were found having run off to Serbia and were brought back and put in the forces of the RS police. Well, this unit was guarding these men at Sandici and one of the members of the unit will testify that he was given an order by his commander after radio contact to murder the 16 people. He said he didn't take part of it but the others did and those people were murdered. It was a unit under Borovcanin's command, clearly organised, and authorised from above after the Kravica warehouse massacres. Okay. Going back to Kravica, I want to show you a photo that -- this is the photo I referred to before that Mr. Borovcanin was standing right in front of this house when these men were looking out like that. If we could go to the still photograph of the video of the Kravica warehouse, and if we don't have it immediately, that's okay. We can come back to it. What happened is Mr. Borovcanin and Mr. Petrovic were on the road and went to the Kravica warehouse with the film running, and the film goes by the warehouse and you see this massive pile of bodies in the front of the warehouse, and the still you can see it from the warehouse. And it goes on, and then you hear automatic gun-fire and you see buses parked in front of the warehouse. And then the film goes black. Now, the Petrovic film was distributed throughout the world to -- when it got to Reuters and others, I believe, but before that Mr. Petrovic gave his copy to a radio -- the I think it's called B-92, the Belgrade -- the famous Belgrade TV station, and they played the section showing the bodies. And then Serbian state security got in and that had not been seen for many years until Mr. Borovcanin in his interviews provided us with that, as did a Dutch journalist. And the copy of this film that was provided, Reuters had the bodies excised and other incriminating things. But you'll get to see at this trial both the excised, edited version, as well as the version that was played over the radio [sic]. So if we could just see a still of that photo. It's resisting, but in any event it was being filmed, the bodies in front of the warehouse, was being filmed in the same vehicle that Mr. Borovcanin was driving. And in his interview he's acknowledged to us that he was there and went by the Kravica warehouse at this time. Of course, he had to. It was on film and it was acknowledged. Everyone knew that he was with Mr. Petrovic, so he didn't have any choice, really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, what's the problem, Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I -- earlier yesterday I objected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, so what?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And I really have to say again that I hate to interrupt my colleague particularly at this moment, but since we really do have the intention to ask for exclusion of Mr. Borovcanin's interview, I would really appreciate it if the Prosecution would not mention what was said in the interviews, otherwise it would cause some prejudice towards Mr. Borovcanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On what legal basis do you maintain that?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Well, if the Prosecution intends to tender Mr. Borovcanin's interview into evidence, well let's just wait for the tenderance of the evidence. We will object to this and are already preparing a written motion with our arguments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see no legal basis for impeding the Prosecution from making reference to the document, which obviously they intend to bring forward because otherwise I don't see any point in making reference to it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could briefly just respond. I have the full and honest belief that this interview was taken completely appropriately under the Rules of the Tribunal, and I anticipate it being entered into evidence, otherwise I would not have mentioned it. I have invited counsel frequently to -- if they intend to challenge a witness statement, a suspect statement -- an accused's statement or there are some significant piece of evidence that they would wish to challenge, that they should do so prior to trial to help us save time. This is the way many adversarial systems are set up. We, unfortunately, do not have those rules and we get by just fine here, but this is the problem it creates. But I think basically if I have a good-faith belief that this can come in, as Your Honours understand that I do, then I will refer to it. I tend to refer to these things fairly briefly. It's not my intention to put on the statement in the opening statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As is being pointed out by my colleague Judge Kwon, exactly, this is a separate matter that will be addressed and determined when it arises. For the time being we just have an intimation of it, but that does not in any way lead to the legal consequence that you should be prohibited or impeded from making reference to it. So go ahead, Mr. McCloskey, and then we'll deal with the matter of the statement when it arises.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Borovcanin is in the vehicle that is filming this and he told the investigator that they went to this area, that his troops were there, his commanders were there, and one of his commanders had burned his hands on a weapon and that he picked up this commander and took him to the Bratunac hospital and did nothing to stop or prevent anything that was going on. Fundamental story. You'll see how the indictment has been built around that, and you'll see the evidence that Borovcanin's troops are all along this road and they are the ones that are in control of the area. Mr. Borovcanin also says the people that are killing these men are Milan Lukic and his men from Visegrad. Milan Lukic is a name that you may recall; he's in custody now. There will be reference that Milan Lukic may have been in the area, but on the 13th of July the men from the Visegrad Brigade's bus had broken down and hadn't made it yet. You'll see that evidence. So Lukic may have been there, but there's no indication that his men were there. There's every indication that the MUP troops, Borovcanin's troops, the 2nd Sekovici Detachment were the ones that were in control of this area. And he was the one that had the power and the ability to stop there; however, as the key commander under Krstic at that time, murder operation had been going on all day long, Krstic had been through that area, there's no question that Borovcanin was updated as part of the murder operation. This killing occurred as part of the murder operation. Now, the issue that you will hear and that you'll have to decide is related to the burned hands because there is -- we have the record, the medical record, of Borovcanin's officer who has burned hands and that are being treated in the Bratunac health centre. And the story, which we don't -- we hear not only from Borovcanin but many people was that the Muslims were gathered in this warehouse, they made a break for it, they grabbed a gun, shot a Serb, and this officer grabbed the Muslim's gun and took it away from him. The other soldiers then opened up on the Muslims and they were all killed. Well, that's the Serb version; it is not the reasonable version. The reasonable version is this: The Serbs decided it was time to kill the people at the warehouse, as they had decided to kill the people at the Jadar River, the Cerska Valley, Nova Kasaba. They put buses in front of the area so that it couldn't be seen from the road so well. They stopped the traffic of the women and children. They got the last man inside the warehouse. They opened fire, and as they opened fire, a Muslim, in a last-ditch effort to save himself, came out of the crowd and took a weapon and fired it, killing a Serb soldier. One of Borovcanin's men did get killed and a Bratunac Brigade Red Beret did get wounded at Kravica. We see the medical records. So this incident with the burned hands took place, we're confident that it did, but not the way that the Serbs say it did. That -- the Serb version is not reasonable. In any event, you'll find that this warehouse is divided into two halves and that one half has probably about 500, the second half has about 500. Even if you look at it under the Serb version, a sudden thing that starts with a few killings, well, it's clear. We have two survivors from this warehouse, one in both sides of the warehouse, as God would give us. And it took hours - you can imagine how long it takes to kill 500 people jammed in two sides of a warehouse, and they'll describe it for you. It took hours. They first of all were shooting at one side of the warehouse and throwing hand-grenades in and then calling people out that survived and shooting them; it went on and on and on. And then after that -- actually, during that time you hear from the other -- the victim that survived the other side. Suddenly he hears all this shooting down the way, and the Serb that's guarding him is saying: Look, see what your people are doing, they're attacking us. Why are they doing that? That doesn't help you. Shortly after all the shooting stopped in the other side of the warehouse, the Serbs go to this side of the warehouse and open up and kill those hundreds of people except this lucky guy that you'll hear from. So even if you look at it from this unreasonable Defence perspective, when Borovcanin is there, he is there while the executions are still going on. Hundreds and hundreds of people are still in the process of being killed. This isn't just some quick response to the Muslims that he -- that's under control and he leaves. He gets there, there's a huge pile of bodies. I think it's on your screen now. This is a huge pile of bodies that's being filmed in the car as he goes by, and you'll see the buses down the road and you'll hear the gun-fire occurring. And he is there at the time, meeting with his commanders that are involved with this; he does nothing. He is the man in control of the area and he does nothing. The killing goes on. They go to the other side of the warehouse. They open up with automatic weapons and hand-grenades. Even there's -- it looks like there's an RPG round that gets thrown in there. And then through the night they are killing individuals that they call out, and they throw hay over the bodies so they can't be seen from the road. And Mr. Borovcanin and his troops are all over this. It's his area, it's the area that he is in charge of and he is in command of and he is responsible for. Now, later on in the evening of the 13th at 2040 hours Mr. Borovcanin has a conversation with General Krstic. This is at the time where most of the men in the warehouse are dead. There are probably still many that are bleeding and slowly dying in the warehouse, and he is now probably, I believe, at the Bratunac Brigade. And so he gets on the phone with General Krstic. "Hello, this is Krstic. "Hello, this is Borovcanin, General. How are you? "Well, where are you, fuck it? "I'm here at the command post. "How's it going? "It's going well. "Don't tell me you have problems. "I don't, I don't. "... went somewhere towards you. "That's exactly what I want to know. "Is there anything special for us from you? "Working on this part ... "Yes. "At the moment. "We'll continue that tomorrow. "All right, man. "Okay. We'll be in touch." Now, do you have any problems? No, I don't. We've just killed a thousand people. That's not a problem. This is a clear indication that General Krstic, who is clearly directing the early parts of this operation -- General Krstic by the evening of the 13th is getting ready for the Zepa assault down in the Zepa area, but is clearly on board and part of the murder operation plan, and so he knows exactly what is going on. And Borovcanin, who has just killed a thousand men, has been part of the killing of a thousand men, is having a nice chat and everything is fine. It clearly shows these men are linked. This is the same evening that Borovcanin's men murdered the 16 people at Sandici field because they were left over and had no way to go. And to show you that this murder was part of an operation that, unbelievably, wasn't that big a deal to some people, I want to show you another document. It's from the 5th Engineering Battalion, dated the 14th of July. It's a regular combat report, and it's from their deputy. I don't think their commander would have been so silly to make a comment like this, but the deputy, Kame Simunic [phoen], did. So this is his regular combat report, reporting on the events that had occurred before, to the Drina Corps command, which of course goes from the Drina Corps then on, and then the Drina Corps reports to the Main Staff. It says: "The enemy: "A large enemy group was infiltrated in the region of Pobudje Brdo and the region of Konjevic Polje." You'll recall that's not far from the area of Kravica. It's the area where the Muslims were turning themselves in. "Units of the 5th Engineering Battalion and the MUP successfully resisted the enemy. About 1.000 to 1.500 enemy civilians and soldiers were arrested and killed." There's no ambiguity there, because on the 14th, when he's writing this, about a thousand to 1.500 Muslim civilians and soldiers are dead and being buried under the supervision of Mr. Beara in this massive grave in Glogova that you will soon see right near Kravica, and there's no other 1.000 or 1.500 killed soldiers. They killed, I'm sure, some going through the woods, but arrested? They first arrested them, then they killed them. Unbelievable document found in the new Drina Corps. The MUP and the army working together precisely. You'll also see that he asked for 50 litres of diesel fuel to help bury them. It's an engineering unit. They had bulldozers. A bulldozer came down from Zvornik to help bury them, as did bulldozers from other areas. It was a joint operation. Mr. Beara. We first see Mr. Beara in the area and involved in an intercept on 13 July at 1009 hours. If you could bring that up. And he's speaking to someone named -- who he refers to Signor Lucic, likely a person from the 65th Protection Regiment. And Beara says: "Do you hear me? Do you know that 400 balijas have shown up in Konjevic Polje?" "Balija" was one of the worst terms that were used against the Muslims. There were other terms. "Turks" was constantly used. "Podarice" [phoen] is another term I have heard used in the Bratunac Brigade reports, but "balija" is one of the more extreme terms that was used. And the person says: "I know. Beara says: "Where are they now? "They came down. Beara: "And they've been rounded up, disarmed, everything?" And Beara says: "Excellent!" They can't hear all the conversation. That's what those dots are. There is modulation problems, there is other issues that you'll hear about, but they write down what they hear. Beara says: "Excellent, excellent, great! And there is someone to guard them, huh? "Yes, there is, there is." Beara: "Good." The guy says: "We have a huge group." And Beara says: "Yeah, well, you can also those 20, so that the forces are not dispersed." Then he says very clearly: "Shove them all on the playground. Who gives a fuck about them?" It speaks for itself. Playground is the soccer field at Nova Kasaba, as far as the investigation can reveal. "Okay, then." Beara says: "They're locked up, right? "Do you have enough room over there? "Well ... "Well, it's not really detention there at your place, it's just - "There's room. And then Beara says: "Yeah. Well, line them up in four to five rows." Now, three or four hours later, if we can go to the next photograph -- well -- this is the playground at Nova Kasaba at about 2.00 on the 13th. This is aerial imagery provided by the United States government and taken from far above the area. And that area outlined in trees is roughly the size of a soccer pitch. And those little dots lined up in rows or lined up in squares are Muslim prisoners, just like Beara had wanted. Can we go back to -- briefly to that intercept. I won't spend a lot of time now on the rest of the intercept, but there is a fellow named Zoka gets on the line, and Zoka is the nickname of Zoran Malinic, the commander of the military police unit that's stationed at Nova Kasaba, and they obviously know each other and they have a bit of an exchange. And Zoka tells Beara about this group that: "Well" -- in the middle of the page: "Well, here it's ... They're killing themselves ... There are also plenty of wounded." Beara says: "You mean they're doing it amongst themselves?" And then you can't hear Zoka, and Beara says: "Uh-huh." And then Zoka says: "They're killing." Beara's response to this is: "Well, excellent. Just let them continue, fuck it." We did have Muslims that committed suicide, both in Potocari, and as they surrendered sometimes they laid on hand-grenades or killed themselves before turning themselves in, so they were indeed killing themselves. And Mr. Beara appears to agree with that. Okay. The next exhibit is from what we call the duty officer's notebook of the Zvornik Brigade. This will be a very important exhibit for you that we will provide to you in a format that will make it very usable. Each of the brigades, the corps, the Main Staff, always had a duty officer. That was one of the top entrusted officers, usually, in the unit that was on the phone and organising and taking care of things always; when the commander was gone, when the commander was there. The duty officer was the person who was the person passing on information and making sure everybody was informed. And sometimes when there's no one else around, the duty officer actually has to make the decisions. So it's an important -- important position. And in the Zvornik Brigade, like elsewhere, they had a little paper notebook where the duty officers would just scratch down little notes. When they got something over the phone, they would, like many of us may have, where they would scratch notes, but it was something that was kept officially because military information is important and sometimes you needed to go back to that. They also had a formal notebook that -- usually where they wrote up the daily combat reports and it was dictated from. But this is the rough notebook. Now, we have that, we have the original. The reason we have it was because, I believe it was 1998, they -- there was an effort made to get the Drina Corps archives out of Bosnia. General Miletic was involved in that, and he was working with Obrenovic to get those documents over to Mali Zvornik across the river. And Obrenovic was allowed to go look at those documents, and he knew he was under investigation at the time, and he managed to grab a bunch of original documents, including this notebook. And when he pled guilty, he gave it to us. Now, we have showed that notebook to many officers of the Zvornik Brigade, and all of them that we have talked to, I believe -- I believe all or almost all have recognised their handwriting in this book, this inked handwriting, and acknowledge that they wrote it. And so this is a very interesting piece of evidence, like this Tribunal may -- it's rare that we get to see this kind of evidence because it's really the note of what's going on at the time. And so I'll go over a bit of that with you so that when it comes up you'll have a basic understanding of it. And it helps give us an idea of where people are and what they're doing and what they're involved in. The first one I would look at would be 13 July. They don't always date the page, so some of the dating has to be done by analysis, but it's not that difficult to figure out. But on 13 July there's a note down at the bottom, sort of the last part, if we could blow that part up. It starts with: "President of the municipality ..." "The president of the municipality, Mitrovic -" it happens to be the president of the Zvornik municipality - "called and asked that a flat-bed trailer -" Colonel Beara crossed out - "be sent to Bratunac to bring a bulldozer 1.000. Colonel Beara passed on the message." The person who wrote this told us that what that meant is he received that message and passed it on to Colonel Beara. The only reason you needed a bulldozer on the 13th of July was to bury bodies and they needed bulldozers to bury bodies we know were being generated along the road and other places. Beara was the man coordinating this effort, so he was the man receiving the information. The next notation, again, is 14 July -- excuse me, is 14 July. That last one was 13 July. And to make it clear, the last three digits of the ERN are 339. And I go to the bottom line: "Colonel Salapura called - Drago and Beara are to report to Golic." Colonel Salapura is the chief of Main Staff intelligence. So it's Tolimir who is intel and security, and then under him is Salapura for intel, Beara for security. As I mentioned, they worked closely together. And Colonel Salapura will be a witness. He was in the area. He won't admit to being part of this, but that's who he is. So he's called on the 14th and he's looking for Drago and Beara. And they're to report to Golic. Now, Golic is Pavle Golic. He is the intel officer at the Drina Corps, who is -- as you'll see from some of the intercepts, is there at the Drina Corps headquarters in Vlasenica coordinating the events, including the operation to murder and bury people. The important part about this is it shows that Drago and Beara are in a unit and they are to report together. In the context of the Zvornik Brigade, well, while Drago is not an uncommon name, when you refer -- when you see "Drago" being referred to, it's Drago Nikolic. You can see by the context, and when you see all the evidence, I'm sure you'll reach that conclusion. And I won't go into a whole lot of detail on that but -- at this time, but that's -- Drago Nikolic was one of the people who was one of the duty officers, even though he didn't want to be because he felt he didn't have to be because he was a security officer, but Pandurevic went out and he had to be a duty officer. And he was during these days. We'll get to that a bit later. Okay. Again on 14th July when Dragan Jokic is duty officer, he gets a call, and the note is at 1000 hours the situation in the battalions is regular. It's -- one of their jobs is to check the different battalions. They had seven battalions at the time, and they would all check in with the duty officer. At 1024 information about Osmaci and the movement of the Muslims. 1500 hours: "Colonel Beara is coming in order to -" blank - "Orovoc, Petkovci, Rocevic, Pilica." It's a misspelling of Orahovac. Petkovci, a little tiny village where the school is where the Muslims are being held. Rocevic, a little tiny village where the school is where the Muslims are being held; Pilica, a little tiny village where the Muslims are being held. This is a direct reference to Beara coming to the Zvornik area to organise the work that needs to be done in relation to these men and these schools. Okay. Another 14 July notation, last three digits of the ERN 346, just going to the middle of the page. Short note: "Beara to call 155." 155 is the Main Staff extension for General Miletic; that's clear from the record. It's Milovanovic's office, but Miletic is now there and you'll see that frequently. And now I think I'll go to the fifth -- let's go to the 15th of July at 0954 hours, and it's the morning of the 15th. Beara is in Zvornik, and there are prisoners that need to be killed at Rocevic and Pilica. Thousands of prisoners. Pandurevic's situation is extreme. He's on his way back at this time. Obrenovic is fully engaged in fighting the column. You know the problems we've discussed with the stretching of the Zvornik Brigade troops, both dealing with the column and dealing with the Muslims. So Beara is not getting any more help from Zvornik, and so he calls General Zivanovic, who had been the corps -- the commander up until the previous night when Mladic, in an impromptu ceremony, retired him and designated Krstic as his commander. The night before this intercept, and that's important. Zivanovic obviously -- excuse me, Beara obviously doesn't know that. And this and the following intercept are crucial intercepts, so I'm going to spend some time, and I apologise, I'm spending more time than I had estimated, but as you can tell, this is very important. So Beara says: "Hello General, sir. "Hello, this is Zivanovic. "Hello. "Hello. "No, that's postponed. "It can't be postponed as long as there are ..." Beara: "Okay there, but that's a new position, a new day, a new ..." And then Beara: "Okay then listen, bro,"

Beara: "I can't do anything without 15 to 30 men with Boban Indjic." Krstic: "Ljubo, this line is not secure." Beara: "I know, I know."
