It was either the Zvornik CSB, Vasic, it could have been Borovcanin, but it was the MUP obviously refused to help. Krstic: "Ljubo, you have to understand me, you guys fucked me up so much." I talked about the two paragraphs related to the prisoners, but then there's another paragraph underneath that says: "I made an offer to the commander of the other side to separate out the civilians and have the others surrender, but he refused, asking that they should all be released together. "The situation is still complicated but under control." Now, at this time Pandurevic did have radio contact with the command of the 2nd Corps folks - I believe it was Semso Muminovic - and they discussed what to do. And Pandurevic apparently made him this offer which the Muslims weren't going to stand for, and so nothing was resolved. But that is a reference to his contact with this 2nd Corps to deal with the Muslim 28th Division is there, coming up. He knows that there are civilians amongst them, he knows there are soldiers. He offered to let the civilians through, to keep the soldiers. There's nothing to do with the Muslim men at the schools. Okay. Just to make sure that's clear. All right. Now, I want to go on to -- we're still with Mr. Beara in an intercept of 16 July at 1111 hours. Ljubo Beara and the one Cerovic. Colonel Cerovic, he is the officer and probably the duty officer of the Drina Corps command in Vlasenica. And Cerovic calls and says: "Hey, listen to me. Triage, report today which ... taken prisoners." X says: "Yes." X says: "To do triage?" Cerovic: "Triage has to be done on the prisoners." Now, on the 16th the only prisoners they have are the some 1.500 to 2.000 in Pilica. X says: "Colonel Beara is right here by me." So we have Colonel Beara at this area which is the Zvornik Brigade, as you'll soon see. "Colonel Beara is right here by me." Cerovic: "Give me Beara." X says: "Go ahead." Beara says: "Yes?" Cerovic says: "Ljubo?" Beara: "I hear you." Cerovic: "Hello! Cerovic speaking." Great radio code discipline. Beara says: "I hear you." And Cerovic says: "Trkulja was here with me just now and he was looking for you. I don't know." Beara: "Yes." Cerovic: "So, he told me ... he got instructions from above." Now, Trkulja is a Main Staff officer who was sent to the Drina Corps to provide information about what to do with the prisoners and at Pilica. And he has stopped by the Drina Corps headquarters. And Beara says: "Yes." And Cerovic says: "To do triage on those." And then he's interrupted. Beara says: "I don't want to talk about it on the phone." Cerovic says: "Okay. Beara says: "Okay, take care." Well, as we know, "triage" is a medical term whereby you separate the wounded who have a chance to live and be treated, and the less -- and treat them first and save the less-serious people until last or the fatal ones not at all. In this context we believe it means a darker impression, that triage means we are to kill the prisoners. Let's go to the next document that will give us a little more information about this, and this is a page out of the duty officer notebook. And from 16 July, the same day as this last intercept, and there's a notation at 1115 hours, and you'll recall the intercept was noted as 1111 hours. So at about the same time -- about the time of this intercept, this notation is made: "It was reported from Zlatar --" that's the Drina Corps headquarters Vlasenica, where Cerovic is the duty officer or on duty -- "that a triage of wounded and prisoners must be carried out and that it was reported to Beara." So this is -- now we know for sure that this conversation is between the Drina Corps and the Zvornik Brigade, that Beara is at the Zvornik Brigade, just in the vicinity of where the prisoners are to be executed. The executions started at Pilica in the morning, probably a bit before this or about this time. All right. Then lastly I want to go to an intercept of August 2nd, and as you recall when we briefly got into the Zepa events, the Zepa men refused to surrender and instead they went wholesale across the Drina to Serbia. They didn't feel they could make it to BiH territory, so they went to Serbia instead. And there was a big effort by the -- Krstic and the Main Staff to get at those people, and this is what this intercept is about between Krstic and Popovic. And Krstic says: "Yes?" Popovic says: "Hey, Boss." Popovic knows who his boss is. Krstic says: "Go ahead." Popovic says: "Beara just called me. He came back from there this morning." Krstic: "Yes." Popovic: "He said he reported to Miletic." Krstic: "Yes." "There are about 500 to 600 of them over there," referring to the prisoners over in Serbia now. Krstic: "Did you understand me, man? What do we have to do with them up there? Popovic: "It's like this. They don't allow anyone to talk with them at all." Krstic: "Is that clear to you, Popovic?" Popovic: "Yes." Krstic: "You and Kosoric straight on to Bajina Basta." Bajina Basta is where they are, that's the town in Serbia right across the river. You remember Kosoric is the intel officer who works closely with Popovic. "Do you know what you're supposed to do?" Popovic: "He tells me: You'll go there for nothing." This means Beara. You'll go there for nothing. Krstic: "Get in touch with that Markovic, the commander of the ... battalion." Popovic: "Yes." "I want you to bring me Turks back here. Is that clear, man?" Popovic: "Well, everything is clear to me, except if they won't give them?" Krstic: "What do you mean, they won't give them? "Well, they won't give them." Krstic: "They're our Turks, man!" Popovic: "Well, the MUP doesn't allow any access." Krstic: "What?" Popovic: "The MUP doesn't allow access, do you understand?" Krstic: "I'll turn the gun barrels on them. Do you understand?" Popovic: "Understood." Krstic: "That's it. Go there as soon as possible." Popovic: "Understood." Krstic: "Go on. "Good. "Bye. "Bye." This is the commander and his security officer dealing with Muslim prisoners that they want to get and bring back to Bosnia. Now, we don't believe they are going to bring back 500 to a thousand people from Serbia and kill them, but they certainly are making a huge effort to get them. This is an indication that of course the Zepa men fled to Serbia, Krstic wants them back. Krstic and Popovic working together as they had done all through the murder operation to deal with prisoners issues. It shows how rabid Krstic is about this, and Popovic is trying to tell him, Look, the Serbs are just not giving them back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, the reference is not correct in 17 two. These are not Popovic words. "I want you to bring me Turks back here." It is Krstic who was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Line 17?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's correct, that's what I said. Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you in agreement in or in disagreement?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said. I guess the transcript -- I've been talking a bit quickly. We are in agreement. That was Krstic, the man that was a bit on the rabid side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So there is no problem. Let's proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So we've switched here to Popovic. Of course Miletic, Krstic, and as well as Beara are involved in this intercept, again showing the same kind of involvement we saw through the murder operation. Now, let me go to Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic, lieutenant commander of the security branch of the Drina Corps. He was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me -- one moment, Mr. McCloskey, just to have this clear in my mind. In this last document that you have been referring to, namely an intercept of August the 2nd, which I understood you were referring to in relation to accused Beara, there is a certain Popovic mentioned who is one of the interlocutors. Is that, according to you, the accused Popovic that we have here or --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I just want to make that clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That is our interpretation of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So as I mentioned, that intercept happened to be one of those documents that wrapped in quite a few people. But now let's go to some examples of the Popovic material. Popovic was with General Krstic on the 11th and Mladic and Pandurevic, and as they came through Srebrenica. So I have a series of photographs just to show you where Mr. Popovic was at certain times. This first photograph is a still from a video that you'll see. You see Krstic on the far left. Popovic is in the tee-shirt with the rifle in his right-hand. Pandurevic is -- that's when Pandurevic is talking to Mladic about getting the Browning up on the top of the hill. And so they're having a bit of a discussion about that, very short. But that shows that Popovic is there with these guys on the 11th of July, involved in the entry into Srebrenica. Okay. The next shot is a shot where on the 12th of July where -- it's after the 12th of July meeting at the Hotel Fontana. General Krstic is giving an interview to the Serb press right across the street from the DutchBat compound, telling the Serb press that all is fine and everyone will be allowed to leave, and there is buses and trucks going by, getting ready to take the women and children away. The men are soon to be separated and the violence is occurring as this video is being shot, but mostly behind buildings and other places at this time, as you'll hear from the DutchBat witnesses. But if you look over the left shoulder of Krstic, you will see Lieutenant -- it's a fuzzy picture, but you'll hear evidence that this is in fact Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic with him on the 12th of July, in Potocari as the events are unfolding. The next photograph. I've got this slightly out of chronology because this occurred just before the last photograph. This is the front of the Hotel Fontana, the morning of the 12th of July, right before the meeting at 10.00 that Mladic had with the Dutch Battalion, with the Muslim representatives, and with various other civilian representatives. This is where Mladic said he wanted to screen people for war criminals, 16 to 60, and he told the Muslims it was up to them whether they wanted to survive or disappear. So right before this meeting these folks, the -- as you look to the left of the screen, the man with his hand on his right hip and the moustache is Momir Nikolic. The man next to him, going to the right, is Radislav Jankovic. He is an intel officer just arrived not long before this from Serbia but is now a senior intel officer with the VRS, and he spoke some English; that's one reason why he was there. Then we have a body-guard of Mladic. And then on the far right we have Vujadin Popovic. Okay. So as we go into the meeting at the Hotel Fontana, you can see Vujadin Popovic drinking the water. As you look at the screen, to his left is a man that I believe is the -- the media affairs officer, Milutinovic. I'm not exactly sure on that right now. That picture is one we've had difficulty identifying. The person at the end of the table is Radislav Jankovic. Going on the other side, the person next to Popovic is Miroslav Deronjic, the head of the party in Bratunac who you'll be hearing from. Then next to Deronjic is Dragomir Vasic, the chief of the CSB Zvornik. Then the person who's -- all we see is the back of his head, is Major Boering of DutchBat, and there is a Muslim woman next to him. But at this key meeting here again we have Popovic. Now, if we could go to a notebook of 15 July, the duty officer's notebook of the Zvornik, last four digits 9356. Thank you. There's a note that the duty officer, Nenad Simic, who was the Zvornik Brigade legal -- morale, legal, and religious affairs person at the time, wrote down this note that Drago and Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic are to report to Major Golic early in the morning. Again, that is Drago Nikolic and Popovic reporting on the work they're doing. And on the 15th of July their work was dealing with the prisoners in the Zvornik Brigade zone and murdering them. Okay. Then a bit later on the 15th, Drago Nikolic took over as duty officer, and we know this from a handwriting example and some other evidence. And so on that same page, if we could blow up the part that says "Requests: 1st Battalion." This is done in Drago Nikolic's hand, and there's a request from the 1st PB, that means 1st Battalion. That is the battalion that is responsible for the area of Pilica, and that's where the some 2.000 prisoners are being held at this time. And they need 50 litres of oil, that's diesel oil, and 20 litres of gasoline. And that's for the transport of troops to Kula. Kula is the school where the prisoners are being held at this time. School -- Kula is this tiny little village, you can hardly call it a village, and there's a school there. So on the 15th of July they're transporting 1st Battalion troops to Kula, and there's only one reason you would transport troops to Kula, and that's to guard the some 1.500 or more Muslims that are there. So here we have the 1st Battalion having to spend resources and time when on the 15th of July the Muslims are hitting them from both sides. This is the problem that Pandurevic was dealing with, but this is his people doing what they have to do to keep these prisoners; not to let them go but to keep them and kill them. There are also ten crates of 7.62 ammunition. Now, 7.62 ammunition is the ammunition that goes in the automatic rifle known as the AK-47 which was the principal rifle used in the mass executions. The ten crates for the 1st Battalion were very likely for the murder operation. The 1st Battalion area is way up north. The column never got there. There wasn't much pressure from 2nd -- from the 2nd Battalion. The mere coincidence that they need that many crates at that time when they're going to need to spend almost all day murdering prisoners, the 10th Sabotage Detachment doing most of the trigger pulling, but with the bullets from Vinko Pandurevic. All right. The next one is 16 July, and if we could -- it is another notebook entry. And this is Milorad Trbic is the duty officer taking these notes down, and if you could blow up the middle part where it starts 0855 hours. "Golic asked Popovic to call him and said that he can forget what he asked for and what he wrote about. He knows what he is supposed to be doing according to the agreed procedure (boss from Panorama 01). Message conveyed to Popovic at 0910." This, remember, is the duty officer notebook from Zvornik, so this means Popovic is in the Zvornik Brigade zone and the duty officer has the ability to convey this message to Popovic. It's not clear what Popovic asked for, but what is clear is that he is told by the superior command that, and I quote: "He knows what he is supposed to do according to the agreed procedure (boss from Panorama 01)." Panorama is the code name for the Main Staff, and when they talk about the commander of a -- whatever unit, they refer to him as 01. So 01 for Zlatar and the Drina Corps is Krstic; 01 for Panorama is Mladic. 01 for Zvornik is Pandurevic. So whatever this is about, Popovic is told on the 16th to get to your job and the procedure that was agreed on by Mladic. And that was conveyed to him, and there is only one thing at this point that Popovic was working on in the morning, and that was organising the murders. Okay. Now -- and related to that we have an intercept. It's dated 16 July, and it's between the Zlatar duty officer and the Palma duty officer. Now, Palma is the code name for Zvornik. They didn't change these names, so these were pretty much present all throughout -- well, a good part of the war, certainly 1995. And what this is about is Popovic needs diesel fuel to carry on the work that he's doing. And fuel at the time in Bosnia was like gold. It was hard to get, and they took very careful accounting of fuel, so the reason this rises to the level of the conversation is because it's such a commodity that is difficult to find and absolutely critical for a murder operation. We have at this time some 1.000, 1.500 people, 2.000 people at the Kula school and the Pilica cultural centre. At 10.00 a.m. they're being bussed and trucked to the Branjevo military farm a few kilometres away. You'll probably get to do this drive if it's not snowing on us, and you need lots of fuel to run buses back and forth, back and forth. A bus takes about 50 people, 60 people, a little more if you really jam them in. But you need fuel for that. This is the work Popovic is doing, and you'll see this when we take a look at this. "Hello, Zlatar. Give me the duty officer. "Yes? "Palma duty officer speaking. 500 litres of D2 for Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic." Zlatar: "For Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic? "Yes." Line disconnects, they have to do it again. "The duty officer at Palma. "Who do you want? "I want to talk to the Zlatar duty officer. "Hello! How did you get connected here? "Hello! Is this Basevic? "What? "Is that Basevic? "Just a moment. "Hello! Is that Basevic? "Yes, it is." Basevic is the logistics officer for the Drina Corps. He's the man that would be distributing fuel. "The guys at Zlatar didn't understand well, I asked for the duty officer, you know? "Yes. "Lieutenant Colonel Popovic is here at Palma, you know?" And the person says: "What?" "Popovic is at Palma." And the person says: "Yes." This is Basevic that says "Yes." And the Palma duty officer says: "500 litres of D2 are urgently being asked for him or else the work he's doing will stop." Now, it's 1358 hours. The murder operation at Branjevo has begun. It's 10:00, 11:00, and it's continuing with the busses going back and forth, back and forth, bringing people to be executed. Basevic: "Well, fuck him, don't you have 500 litres of oil? They're asking for 2 tons loaded. "Well, I don't know. He just called me from the field and told me to pass you the message over there." From the 1st Battalion near Pilica, you can't call directly on a military line to the Vlasenica-Drina Corps headquarters; you've got to go through the line that they have directly to the Zvornik Brigade headquarters where you get the duty officer. That's why there is this exchange going on. Then Basevic: "Two tons of oil are arriving now at your place ... You can't find oil. Should I deliver them to you by helicopter? "Well, then, get in touch with Rosevic." I don't know what that means. "Is Major Golic there, by chance? "Yes. "Let me talk to him." So now Palma now wants to talk to Golic, who we've heard about. "Golic, Pop --" That's Popovic's nickname. You'll hear it a lot. "Golic, Pop just called me and told me to contact you. 500 litres of D2 have to be sent to him immediately, otherwise his work will stop. Yeah, man. Yeah, 500 litres or else his work will stop. Go on, right away. "Bye." Immediately after the end of this conversation Palma says: "A bus loaded with oil is to go to Pilica village. That's it." So, yes, there's been a reference to his work; yes, we know he's in Zvornik; and now we know the oil is to go to Pilica village, 500 litres. "No, it should go with its fuel tank from the vehicle battalion. "So it's separate? "Yes, yes, it should be separate. "There is, but Lieutenant-Colonel Krsmanovic over at your place has to call the vehicle battalion here." Krsmanovic is a Drina Corps logistics guy. Okay, so at the very same time as this intercept, let's now go to the duty officer notebook. It's the next exhibit. And there's a notation at 1400 hours, and you'll recall this intercept was 1358 hours. So again Trbic is the duty officer. "At 1400 hours Popovic requested a bus with a full tank and 500 litres of D2. Zlatar duty officer and Golic informed." So these two intercepts put together with a reference to Pilica and what we know is going on is an absolute smoking gun. It shows beyond any reasonable doubt that Popovic is involved in doing his job, which is organising for the transportation of the Muslim men from Kula to be murdered at Branjevo. There's also another document, it's a Zvornik receipt document that actually is the receipt for 500 litres of fuel with Popovic's name on it and Pilica mentioned again. Absolutely solid evidence, clear, unambiguous that this man is doing his job, transporting people to their deaths. Okay. Another entry from the book, the notebook. This is on 16 July, and this is a message -- it's noted down in the middle of the -- in this notebook that there's a message from Zlatar that Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic must go to Vinko Pandurevic in the field at 1640 hours. The message through the 1st Battalion that Popovic must report to the duty officer so he can be sent on to a task by Zlatar. So this shows us that Popovic is indeed at the 1st Battalion area because that's where messages are being sent to get to him, and it shows that Zlatar has something in mind for him and that he must go to see Pandurevic in the field. Now, you'll hear from other evidence that this is about the time that -- that Vinko Pandurevic had opened up a corridor for the Muslim column to go through, and this information went out, leaked out through the police, and was -- eventually found its way to the Main Staff, to the president's office. And so you'll see the evidence that the Main Staff is -- and the president are very concerned that someone has opened a column up and -- or -- and let them through. And Pandurevic did this on his own without approval, after, as I mentioned yesterday, some 50 of his troops and MUP soldiers were killed in this massive swarm of people. And the Drina Corps and the Main Staff want reliable information of what is going on, and so who do they -- to see what this commander may be up to, and so who do they send but a security officer. Naturally they are the ones who are looking into what commanders do. So they have Popovic in the field, they get him, they send him out to the forward command post, away from his job at Pilica, where he actually sees some of the results of this awful battle, and he reports back on the results up to the corps and about how awful it was. And he also talks about -- a bit in that conversation about the murder operation. But that's what that's about, but that provides us important information about the whereabouts of Popovic, what he's doing, what Vinko Pandurevic is doing, and ties in to the genocide in that the Main Staff, the corps, wanted to get everybody. They did not want this column out. They could not understand why anybody would open a column. Pandurevic was faced with the reality of more deaths of his soldiers, opened up the column, and told his people about it later. And as you'll see, the Main Staff sent some senior officers a day or two later to find out and investigate this because they weren't at all pleased, but as a result I think they came back satisfied that Pandurevic, under the circumstances, had done the right thing by opening up the column. Okay. Mr. Nikolic, as you recall, or may recall from yesterday, we first see Mr. Nikolic when he calls Dragan Obrenovic from the forward command post and says: I've just received a call and the Muslim -- thousands of Muslims prisoners are coming. We have to house them and kill them. And I won't go through that with you again. But, as I said, he was able to be relieved and go attend to his duties to the Muslim prisoners. And if we go to what is called the forward command post log-book, the Drina -- the Zvornik Brigade has a forward command post and they keep a log-book, and we have translated the sections that appear to be relevant. We note -- and I'll take you to that exhibit now. 13 -- if you could blow up that middle one, Janet, that's 13 July, and it's Major Galic who is one of the officers of the Zvornik Brigade. And he writes: "I took over duty (unscheduled) from Lieutenant Drago Nikolic at 2300 hours. "Last night was relatively quiet with individual attacks by enemy forces from" these various places, "but there were no losses or damages." So what we see is in the evening, after the time Obrenovic tells us he receives the call, we actually have Major Galic making an unscheduled substitution for Drago Nikolic, corroborating Dragan Obrenovic's testimony, and it's clearly a normal reaction. They've got hundreds of Muslim prisoners that are now arriving - we know that from a survivor - and Nikolic has to go deal with it. So he gets an unscheduled relief from a very important post, the forward command post. Okay. The next -- next document is a log-book entry for a vehicle that belongs to the military police. And if we could -- that's the front of it, showing that it's a Zvornik Brigade military police book, but if we could go to the next section. That's the blank one, it should be the next one after that that actually talks about the dates. And if we could blow up the 13 July part, both pieces. There are two 13 July. Thank you. And it shows this vehicle on the 13th of July going to the little village of Orahovac, then to Zvornik, and then back to Orahovac, then Standard, which is the name of the Zvornik Brigade headquarters, then down to Bratunac. Bratunac where, 13th of July, you know the -- the prisoners are being -- are being held. They have not been transferred en masse yet until the evening of the 13th, and this is -- shows the involvement that the MPs are obviously having at key locations. And if we go on to the next page that shows the 14th through the 17th, this becomes very clear. Here's another shot, but it's the same vehicle and it's just a continuation, if you go to the next page. If we could blow up basically the 14th through the 17th, if that's possible. If you look at the trips, you'll recognise Standard -- on the 14th: Standard-Orahovac, Orahovac-Rocevic, Orahovac-Zvornik, Standard-local. 14th of July, that's when the prisoners are there, being killed. Prisoners are going to Rocevic at the same time. 15 of July, Karakaj-Rocevic-Local-Standard-Divic-Zvornik. Now, 15 of July, Rocevic, that's the key time for Rocevic. Then we look also at the 15 of July Standard-Kozluk. That's where people are being killed. Standard-Rocevic-Kozluk. So they're all over Kozluk and Rocevic, these tiny little places, on the key day that people are being killed. So they're monitoring that. 16 of July, Kula, a tiny little village next to Pilica. Local-Standard-Kozluk, that's where they're being buried at that time. Rocevic, maybe there's prisoners still at the school. Pilica, back to Pilica on the end of the day. 17 July they go down to Kravica. I don't know why they're going down there then. Now, I can't put Drago Nikolic in this vehicle, but it's clearly a military police or security vehicle. He would be directing the military police. He would know what they're up to and what they're involved in. It would be his job to direct them and organise them, and you'll hear from some of these military police officers that have identified Drago Nikolic at Orahovac and involved in these events. Another document related to the military police is a roster which I will show you a photocopy of the Serbian version, or the Zvornik Brigade version, a partial part of it. Not that section, but it's the one with the names. I think you've got it. There. Okay. This is a roster of the military police company that Drago Nikolic had responsibilities over, and what you'll see from an expert report, and I'll show the actual original document. We don't normally need to bring in original documents, but this one I will bring in for you unless we get a stipulation. This shows about 12 to 14 members of the military police on the day of 14 July, and you can see in the original version that the lettering that's noted in the box has been changed. And from O to T. And then on the back of the document you'll see a little legend, and it's -- T is terrain, which means being out in the field, and then you see erased by pencil erasures O/Orahovac. So what we see in this document is about 12 or 14 MPs that are -- have been -- originally had an O next to their name at Orahovac, it's been erased, and T has been put over the top. And then I think there's six or seven on the next day, the 15th, where R has been erased and T has been put over the top of that, and that means -- R is for Rocevic and they put T over the top. This is the unit that Drago Nikolic is responsible for. This is a clear indication -- and you'll hear from testimony of people that were there at Orahovac, that they were there and this is an effort to cover up all of which Drago Nikolic would have known about and been part of. All right. One last document that I'm not going to go into in detail, and that is the -- a document related to the -- the story I told you about. This document is dated 26th July. It's under the hand of Drago Nikolic, and it's to the military prosecutor in Bijeljina. It's about -- it's entitled: "Collaboration with enemy, report, delivered to." And then it goes into explaining how, after Srebrenica, these people were captured and they were assisted by a couple of Zvornik officers and that they -- and then they were prosecuted. This is one of many documents related to that very grim affair, where, after being used as witnesses against Serbs, these men were killed. Drago Nikolic was part of that, he knew about it, he's responsible for it. This also shows us that there is an active system in place to punish people for doing wrong. And I haven't said anything about it at this point, but -- and I won't say much. But they had a clear system in place to prosecute wrong-doers. No one was ever prosecuted for this. Vinko Pandurevic did nothing to prosecute or investigate or anything. Neither did Mr. Borovcanin. It was their duty to do so; they did not. It's clear as a bell. So that ends the -- many of the critical documents of the case. Where this case will largely be tried, these documents, these intercepts, the testimony from the various witnesses, especially the insider witnesses that will go directly to the acts or conduct of the accused. But let me just say some final words. When criminal orders originate from the top, they spread downward like a disease, infecting most of all the people in positions of power and authority, tasked with carrying out those orders. It doesn't have to be that way because following criminal orders is not an imperative. A soldier becomes infected when he does so under his own free will. It is not like a disease, it's not infectious. You do it when you choose to do it. A soldier, especially an officer, is different. He is first and foremost a creature of duty, a creature of honour, and a creature of code. There is no important human job in our society [sic]. They are the men that protect us and protect our homes, and they live by a very strict and important code that this Tribunal is mandated to enforce. These men received that training; they know the difference between good and evil. They chose wrongly. Their duty tells them loudly and clearly that they must not embrace criminal orders. Every soldier has a choice. He can pick up the phone or the gun and do the bidding of men like Mladic, or he can choose not to follow the orders and stand down. Call the ICRC, get out of town, ruin your career. This, of course, creates a tremendous strength of character and courage, none of which these accused in court today possessed. Where they lost their honour, I don't know. Probably early on in this ethnic war. Only they know that. When you're considering the issue of intent, please remember each of these men wilfully and voluntarily chose to support these awful crimes with the knowledge that their contribution would play a significant and crucial role in the commission of those crimes. The only way we will get into the minds of these accused is through their actions and statements. Your Honours, I believe you may - in fact should, based on the evidence - infer that these men intended the known results of their conduct. The evidence in this case will provide you with no reasonable alternative. This is not a case of mere aiding and abetting. If this Tribunal is to stand up to impunity, it must require that men are responsible for their actions. Okay. In conclusion, I want to take you briefly back to the victims to remind us all again why we're here in the first place. To do this, I want to share with you the words of a woman from Srebrenica named Mirsada Malagic, whose words I will never forget. She testified in the Krstic case. Near the end of her testimony Judge Rodriguez told her that she would have to stay another day, as you know that happens, and he suggested she go out and see a bit of The Hague, and so she did that. And when she came back and finished her testimony, this is what she told us. Think about genocide when you hear what she said. "Yesterday afternoon when I returned from here, I went out to walk around your city. That is what I wanted to tell you. I couldn't really see much, but what I really liked, what caught my eye, was a monument that we visited, and that monument was to women, that is, women awaiting sailors who never came back. And the monument to those wives touched me profoundly. I should like to find this statue and take it to Bosnia with me. Perhaps it could be likened to mothers and wives of Srebrenica who have been waiting and hoping for all those years, except that we followed different roads. We could turn to our empty forest. We saw our sons, our husbands off to those woods and never found out anything about them again, whether they were alive or dead, where their bones are lying. Many mothers have died hoping against hope, and it's quite possible that all the mothers would end up like that because their numbers are dwindling every day." Mirsada lost her husband Salko, her two sons Elvir and Admir - Admir was only 16 - her father-in-law Omer, both Salko's brothers Osman and Jaspur, her nephew Samir, and this wasn't unusual. Many lost and suffered more. The loss of these men and boys and the crippling of those left behind can be simply put: This is a Bosnia genocide we must never forget. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Just one moment so that we will discuss something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ostojic, are you in a position to start now? And continue tomorrow, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I would prefer to start in the morning, as I said, but I'll do as the Court wishes. Whatever your pleasure is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ostojic. Perhaps you can go on today for about 30 minutes, and then we stop because we would need to have a break for the staff in any case. And then you will resume tomorrow. Is that acceptable to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's acceptable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I would just ask if I can get a podium to place my paperwork on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That would help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, could you please assist Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is this normal? I don't recall having to share one podium between Prosecution and Defence. Okay. All right. Thank you. And Mr. Ostojic also is tall.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. As you know, my name is John Ostojic, and I'm here representing Mr. Ljubisa Beara. Good afternoon to my learned colleague at the Office of the Prosecution, and to my colleagues at the Defence table. We have heard some comments from the Prosecution today, and with the Court's indulgence, I will take off the head-sets. I will try to follow as much as possible. We're here for two reasons: One obviously that was expressed yesterday and today in some of the closing remarks, and that is to express our sympathy to the victims, the families, and the friends of the people who died in Srebrenica in 1995. It's undisputed that July, 1995, was a tragic, horrific time which caused senseless loss of lives on all sides. It was a war that the Prosecutor himself acknowledges may have been legitimate to a certain extent. There was a war that was going on there since 1992. We are not here and we would never attempt to minimise the tragedy or the pain and suffering experienced by these victims, their families, or their friends. We are here also, however, to the extent possible, to seek the truth, the truth about, at the very least, Mr. Beara. The truth that you have not heard thus far, quite candidly, the truth that we wish through the evidence, with your patience and your guidance that you all will hear at the conclusion of our evidence in this case. We respectfully ask that each defendant be judged solely on their conduct, not to judge all of them, as the Madam Prosecutor yesterday told us, with this collective guilt; however, in my opinion, from looking at the web that was weaved by the Prosecution, there is a sense of collective guilt that they're trying to prove by lumping parties together and lumping people together. We ask that the Court respectfully, as I'm sure and confident that you will, do not - and I repeat do not - utilise this theory of collective guilt. It's my view that when we judge someone or anyone, specifically Mr. Beara - I always mispronounce his name; I apologise - that we in fact, in order to know a man, in order to understand a man, in order to glean what a man or a person is all about, we don't start with an intercept or we don't start with a document that I'll discuss later may have some flaws and quite candidly has many flaws within it and subject to numerous interpretation. But to judge a man we must learn first about his biography. What is he about? Where was he born? Where does he come from? What was his education and upbringing like? What was his family situation like? To know about Mr. Beara, we covered some of his biography in our pre-trial brief, but I'll share it again with you in a general overview. We expect that the evidence will show, through witnesses, specifically why this is both relevant and important. But if you're going to judge a person, respectfully, we must know that person in greater detail than in just the three days that the Prosecution is alleging that he participated in these horrific crimes. We believe that with Mr. Beara's background and biography, the Court will be convinced that he could not and did not possess the criminal intent necessary for the crimes alleged, specifically genocide, extermination, murder, persecution, deportation, and any other war crimes during the time at issue. Mr. Beara was born on July 14th, 1939, a significant date, we believe. He was born in Sarajevo, in former Yugoslavia, Bosnia and Herzegovina. He completed and was brought up, completing both grammar school and high school in Sarajevo. His father, Jovan, was a second lieutenant in the Royal Army before World War II. His father was captured in 1941 and was a prisoner of war in Germany for four years, until 1945. Mr. Beara's father, Jovan, was re-activated into the JNA and became a major in the air force. His family comes from a small village called Bare, very similar spelling to his last name, but it's B-a-r-e. It's in Sinj in Croatia. Mr. Beara grew up and was taught by his military father never to discriminate, never to hold biases or to have prejudice against any peoples. Mr. Beara grew up and followed in his father's footsteps. Mr. Beara was not a Serb nationalist; he was a Yugoslav, someone who believed in the multi-ethnic, multi-ethnic structure of that former country, being born and growing up in Croatia, living in Sarajevo, following his father's footsteps as a Yugoslav officer. Mr. Beara attended the Military Maritime Academy from 1959 to 1963, following in his father's footsteps of honour, code, and duty. In 1973 he was designated as the chief security officer for the military coast region in Split, Croatia, which covered not only the coast area, but a large inland section of approximately 75 kilometres. In 1985, Mr. Beara obtained the rank of a naval captain. He never became an admiral, stayed at the level of a naval captain. I believe the evidence will show that the naval captain is the equivalent of a colonel. So from 1985 the evidence will show that Mr. Beara has not been promoted and has not been elevated to any military position other than the one he maintained approximately ten years prior to the events that we're here discussing at this trial. We believe that is significant for two reasons: One, the Prosecution suggests that it's significant, but not for Mr. Beara. They took portions of their theories and apply it differently. If it's significant for all accused, it should be significant for Mr. Beara that he was not promoted. It is indicative of certain things, and we hope that when our Defence case comes through, you will find why we feel it is important. From 1992, Ljubisa Beara was stationed in the Crna Rijeka as a staff officer in the Main Staff of the VRS. His rank at that time was changed from a naval captain to a colonel, which is essentially a parallel ranking in the different systems after 1992. Ljubisa Beara is married and has been married since September 23rd, 1962. He has two sons and two grandchildren. I believe the evidence will also show that bringing up those two young men and his two grandchildren, he has never shown them or tried to teach them discriminatory prejudice or to be biased against any peoples but has continuously looked at all people equally. We believe the evidence will show, just by the background, as I've stated earlier, that Mr. Beara cannot and did not possess the criminal intent necessary, not just for genocide, not just for extermination and murder, but also for persecution where you need an elevated intent of discriminatory intent. I'll only highlight some of his background now and bring forth testimonials and evidence to this Trial Chamber when I'm given that opportunity. Professionally and personally, there were many victims of the war in former Yugoslavia. In 1992, Mr. Beara also personally and professionally had a setback, many setbacks, but professionally speaking one of the main setbacks that Mr. Beara had, which is what we believe the evidence will show, indicated a detachment from the Serbs because of Mr. Beara's background. In 1992, as I'm sure the Prosecution knows and as the evidence will show, in approximately April through June of 1992, there was a killing of two paramilitary soldiers. In 1992, these two paramilitary soldiers apparently tried to take a VRS transport vehicle. At the time, they were able to seize this transport vehicle and take it. Subsequent to that, the men who -- the military men who were going to retrieve the military vehicle, transport vehicle, there was a gun battle. Two soldiers, two paramilitary soldiers, died. Mr. Beara was accused of participating in the killing of those two soldiers in a transport vehicle. Now, you might be wondering how is it related. We believe the evidence will show that on that April, 1992, date when those two paramilitary soldiers were shot killed -- shot and killed, blame was placed on Mr. Beara, a staff security officer. At that time, Mr. Beara spent 47 days in jail awaiting his trial in order to prove his case. After three trials, several appeals, at each of the trials Mr. Beara was vindicated. He was found not guilty of those killings. But that is not where the evidence stops with respect to this 1992 incident. What's important about the incident and why we believe it reflects the start of a detachment for Mr. Beara is the fact that we don't know or haven't yet told you who were those two paramilitary soldiers who stole the military transport? They were not Muslim, they were not Croats; they were Serbs. Mr. Beara at that time was being charged with a crime for killing two Serb paramilitary soldiers who stole a Serb vehicle. He was being prosecuted not by Croats, not by Muslims, but by Serbs. Mr. Beara's run-in with the law, respectfully similar to this, also occurred approximately one year and three months later -- one year and five months later. It's an action that's been reported as the September, 1993, action. It's significant, we believe, because the military, as the Prosecutor seems to suggest, is very strict in discipline, follows many specific rules and codes. At this point in 1992 we suggest that there was a loss of confidence in Mr. Beara and he was moved off to the side. He became a member of the Main Staff security unit with no personnel, with no troops to command, and with no authority vested in him at any time from 1992 through well beyond July, 1995. This is one reason, we suggest - and we believe the evidence will prove - why he was isolated and detached from all the events that happened here. 1993, as I started to say, the incident is called the September 1993 action. We hope to bring evidence, and we will with respect to the July -- or with the 1992 incident, bring the Prosecutor, and I believe a Judge we're bringing as well, to verify and substantiate what I'm telling you, and we have documents to support that. September 1993 action is a relatively well-known incident reported primarily, though, in the former Yugoslavia. What was September 1993 action? It was an action purportedly set up to make a military coup against President Radovan Karadzic. Again, who was implicated in the September 1993 action? Unfortunately, Mr. Beara. We suggest, as we did with the 1992 incident, that that event is also relevant and important, both from a military standpoint and from a personal standpoint, to show and reveal that Mr. Beara was actually detached and not closely linked, as the Prosecutor seems to suggest, but detached from the events involving Srebrenica in July of 1995. I failed to mention with respect to the 1992 incident, Mr. Beara did get punished for that, not only spending 47 days in jail, but he also was sanctioned for using what they considered to be inappropriate language when he was advising or telling his men to retrieve the transporter with these two Serb paramilitary officers -- soldiers. He used words that Mr. McCloskey says are derogatory, and indeed they are. There's no dispute about that. But when you see that evidence, you'll see that he used those same derogatory words against the Serbs, and he got punished with a six-month to a one-year probationary period because the witnesses testified and said he shouldn't use derogatory words, although he did, and it may have been custom and practice, not to the extent the Prosecution suggests that there is a meaning to those word, but just in general colloquy between officers, or between staff officers or between people. I hope we don't judge Mr. Beara or any individual, on using either profanity or using a derogatory word, because that, I believe, is not what this Tribunal is set up to be and that, I believe, is not what any criminal institution is set up to be. But you'll find that Mr. Beara did use derogatory words, both against Serbs and supposedly or purportedly against Muslims, as Mr. McCloskey expects to prove in his evidence -- in his case. I believe it's insignificant. I don't believe using those words really indicate what one person feels about one ethnic group or another. It certainly should not be used. It certainly is something we try to deter and refrain from doing, but unfortunately it happens from time to time, but I don't believe it reaches a criminal level of culpability or responsibility. Mr. Beara's personal and professional life, his detailed biography alone, and the two incidents we've discussed thus far proves that he did not at any time have the power, the control, or the authority to do any of the crimes that are alleged by the Prosecution. We believe that he was detached. And if you look at the evidence of the Prosecution, even the evidence that they gleaned here with us today about Mr. Beara, you'll find that there are reasonable interpretations for each of the documents. But not just reasonable, more plausible. More plausible and perhaps even truthful explanations as to what the documents suggest and really meant to be. I don't accept the intercepts, and I'll tell the Court why when we file our motion, when the evidence comes in. We don't believe they are reliable. We don't accept them as being truthful in all cases. And, quite frankly, if you look at, by way of example, one intercept that the Prosecutor tried -- or showed you today, that was the intercept between Mr. Beara and Mr. Krstic. Beara says on the lower part of that transcript: "I've been waiting three days." If it's true that Mr. Beara said he's been waiting three days, on the 15th does it not indicate clearly enough that he's done nothing for three days? Not according to the Prosecutor, because it doesn't fit into his web of collective guilt. If it's true that Mr. Beara is on that intercept, he plainly says: "I've been waiting three days." Nothing has happened. We'll go into more of the specific evidence tomorrow of what we believe the security staff officer, Mr. Beara, was doing and how he was doing it. But I'd like to just, with the last couple minutes, just address the Court in this if I may: We think that the evidence will prove that an acquittal is not only a fair and honest result, but it would be the correct decision, most respectfully, as it relates to Mr. Beara. I address only him because I represent him and believe that the evidence should stand or fall with each of the accused and not in a total vacuum. The evidence will prove that not every Serb in the world is guilty of war crimes. The evidence will prove that not every male Serb is guilty of war crimes in Srebrenica. The evidence will prove that not every male Serb military person is guilty of war crimes in Srebrenica. The evidence will prove that in fact not every Serb military staff officer in the security unit is guilty of war crimes, and I respectfully believe and have the conviction and look forward to share with you that the evidence will prove that Mr. Ljubisa Beara is not guilty of the crimes charged by the Prosecution. I'm not sure if it's a good point to stop. I may continue, but -- thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's perfect, Mr. Ostojic. The understanding is we will reconvene tomorrow morning at 9.00. Mr. Ostojic will continue and finish his opening statement, to be followed by the Defence for Mr. Nikolic. If there is a time to spare, then, Mr. Gvero, we will ask you to make your statement, as per your wish expressed during the pre-trial conference. How long do you think you will require for your statement? How much time?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED GVERO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think that the indication we gave was half an hour, but it seems that 10 to 15 minutes would be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Mr. Gvero. You may sit down. So the understanding is please prepare yourself for your statement tomorrow because it's very likely that it will -- it will take place tomorrow. And that's it. So I think we should cover all the remaining territory tomorrow and then start with the first witness on Thursday. In the meantime, we are sure we'll have ready our decision on protective measures because it relates also in part to the first witness. Thank you, good afternoon, and see you tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 23rd day of August, 2006, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.23 p.m.,
